opus-5.5.text:
I think the most realistic near-term goal is to get a robot that can reliably do a meaningful range of tasks in one real, semi-structured setting, rather than a robot that can do everything everywhere.

There's a lot of excitement right now. People see a vision-language-action model fold a shirt or pick up a cup in a demo video and assume general-purpose household robots are just around the corner. But a demo and a product are very different things. A demo needs a success rate that looks good on camera. A product needs something like 99% reliability, robustness to lighting changes, to objects it has never seen, to people walking around, and it needs to recover when it makes a mistake. That gap is enormous, and closing it is the real work of the next few years.

So in the near term, I would focus on a few things.

**Generalizable manipulation skills.** Picking, placing, opening, retrieving. If a robot can grasp almost any object in a retail store, a pharmacy, or a factory warehouse, across thousands of SKUs it has never seen, that alone is very valuable. These skills are also the building blocks for longer, more complex tasks.

**Data.** The core bottleneck for embodied intelligence is data, not model architecture. Language models had the whole internet. We don't have an internet of robot actions. Teleoperation data is high quality but very expensive and slow to scale. That's why I put a lot of weight on synthetic data and simulation: generating large amounts of physically plausible training data, learning the foundational skills there, then using a smaller amount of real-world data to close the sim-to-real gap. I think the realistic path is a pyramid: massive synthetic data at the bottom, internet video and human data in the middle, and a thin layer of real robot data on top.

**Hierarchy.** I don't believe one end-to-end model will soon handle everything from "what does the user want" down to joint torques at high frequency. A more realistic architecture has a large vision-language model doing understanding and planning, plus specialized, fast, reliable skill models executing actions. Over time these layers can merge, but for deployment right now, structure gives you reliability and debuggability.

**Getting into real deployment and building a flywheel.** Once robots are actually working in a commercial setting, even a narrow one, they generate real data about failure cases, and that data makes the model better. Without that loop, you're stuck optimizing benchmarks in the lab.

So my honest answer is: within the next few years, the goal is to have embodied robots doing genuinely useful work in specific commercial scenarios, with high reliability and the ability to generalize to new objects and environments within that scenario. Not general household robots yet. That's a longer journey. But if we can make the step from "impressive demo" to "it actually works every day and someone is willing to pay for it," that's the milestone that would show embodied intelligence is becoming real.

r001.rationale: The response says general-purpose household robots are a longer journey, but does not judge a fully general vision-language-action model within one or two years to be impossible.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes commercial deployment and useful paid work in specific scenarios, but does not identify finding a commercialization model that can be replicated at scale as a central current goal.

fable-5.1.text:
I think a realistic near-term goal is not a general-purpose robot that can walk into any home and do anything. That is the long-term dream, but if we are honest about where the models are, I would frame the next two to three years differently.

The first realistic goal is getting a VLA model to generalize across objects, scenes, and lighting within a bounded set of skills. Picking, placing, opening, pouring, folding, that kind of thing. Today a lot of demos look impressive, but if you move the table ten centimeters or change the cup, success rates fall off quickly. Getting robust, say ninety-plus percent success on a few dozen manipulation skills in unseen environments would already be a major achievement, and it would be enough to unlock real deployments in logistics, light manufacturing, and some service settings.

The second goal is on the data side. In language, the internet gave us essentially free pretraining data. In robotics we do not have that. So the question is how we build a data flywheel. I think the realistic answer is a mix: large-scale simulation with good physics and rendering, human video as a weak but abundant signal, and a smaller amount of real teleoperation data to ground everything. If in the next few years we can show a clear scaling law, where adding more of this mixed data reliably improves real-world performance, that changes how the whole field invests.

The third goal, which people underestimate, is the hardware-software interface. Dexterous hands are still a bottleneck. A model can only be as capable as the body it controls, and tactile sensing, reliability, and cost all matter. I would like to see hands that can do in-hand manipulation at a price point where a university lab or a mid-sized company can afford a fleet, not just one unit.

So if you ask me what success looks like around 2028 or so, I would say: a few thousand robots doing useful, repetitive manipulation tasks in real commercial environments, driven by a shared foundation model, learning from each other's data. Not a humanoid butler. But a system where the loop is closed, deployment generates data, data improves the model, the model expands to new tasks. Once that loop is actually turning, the longer-term goals become an engineering problem rather than a research question.

r001.rationale: The response calls a general-purpose robot a long-term dream and frames a two-to-three-year goal around bounded skills, but it does not say that achieving a fully general VLA model within one or two years is impossible.

r002.rationale: The response mentions useful commercial deployments and thousands of robots, but it does not identify finding a replicable, scalable commercialization model as a central current goal.

astra-6.text:
I think a realistic near-term goal is to get robots to reliably complete useful tasks in a bounded environment. For example, can a robot handle a range of pick-and-place tasks, even when the objects, their positions, or the instructions change? And when something goes wrong, can it recognize the failure and recover?

For vision-language-action models, the interesting question is whether we can transfer what a model learns across tasks and environments, so that each new application requires less data and less engineering. We don’t need to jump straight to a robot that can do everything. A meaningful step is a system that can do a limited set of useful things consistently, adapt to modest changes, and ask for help when it reaches its limits.

r001.rationale: The response says there is no need to jump straight to a robot that can do everything, but it does not judge a fully general VLA model within one or two years to be impossible.

r002.rationale: It discusses reliable bounded tasks, transfer, and reduced data and engineering, but does not identify a replicable commercialization model at scale as a central goal.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a realistic near-term goal is to get a robot to reliably complete a useful task in a reasonably constrained environment. For example, can it understand a request, find the relevant objects, and carry out a sequence of manipulation actions—and recover when something goes wrong? A compelling demonstration is a starting point, but we need to measure how consistently it works across different objects and conditions.

For vision-language-action models, the opportunity is to bring broad visual and language understanding into physical behavior. The challenge is that understanding what should happen doesn’t automatically mean knowing how to execute it. So I would focus on improving that connection, with clear tasks and repeatable evaluation, and then gradually expanding the range of situations the robot can handle.

r001.rationale: The response describes a constrained near-term task and gradual expansion, but does not judge a fully general model within one or two years to be impossible.

r002.rationale: It calls for useful tasks and repeatable evaluation, but does not identify finding a commercialization model that can scale through replication as a central goal.
